title: MeshSlice: Efficient 2D Tensor Parallelism for Distributed DNN Training
problem: One-dimensional tensor parallelism (1D TP) for large DNN training scales poorly because all-reduce communication cost grows linearly with the number of devices. Existing 2D TP algorithms for general matrix multiplication (GeMM) have fundamental inefficiencies: Cannon's algorithm generates high traffic, SUMMA suffers from synchronization overhead, and 2D GeMM with standard collective communication operations cannot overlap communication with computation.
method: MeshSlice introduces a new 2D GeMM algorithm that decomposes collective communication operations into multiple smaller partial collectives, each of which can be issued and overlapped with ongoing matrix-multiply computation on the local shard. The algorithm maps the 2D device mesh such that partial all-reduces along one mesh dimension are issued while the other dimension is computing, hiding most communication latency behind arithmetic. An analytical autotuner searches over 2D mesh shape (rows x columns), GeMM dataflow configuration, and communication granularity (number of slices) to find the Pareto-optimal configuration for each LLM layer and cluster size, targeting TPUv4 hardware with its torus interconnect.

title: SAGA: A Memory-Efficient Accelerator for GANN Construction via Harnessing Vertex Similarity
problem: Graph-traversal-based Approximate Nearest Neighbor (GANN) construction faces severe memory bottlenecks due to high-dimensional vertices and dynamic graph updates. Existing accelerators like NDSearch struggle with the massive pre-processing overhead required for dynamic graph scenarios.
method: SAGA exploits vertex feature similarity by clustering vertices with the same starting point during the initial construction step. It decomposes vertices into key and non-key types with delta values in a narrow range, enabling mixed-precision quantization. A specialized two-level scheduling architecture with a bit-serial mixed-precision unit implements efficient GANN construction.

title: Scalable Community Detection Using Quantum Hamiltonian Descent and QUBO Formulation
problem: Community detection in large-scale graph data is computationally expensive with classical optimization; existing approaches lack scalability for diverse graph sizes and structures.
method: The approach reformulates community detection as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problem and applies Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD) to find optimal community structures. A multi-level algorithm iteratively refines community assignments by alternating between QUBO setup and QHD-based optimization.

title: PAPI: Exploiting Dynamic Parallelism in Large Language Model Decoding with a Processing-In-Memory-Enabled Computing System
problem: LLM decoding kernels dynamically shift between memory-bound and compute-bound behavior as request parameters (batch size, sequence length, sampling strategy) change at runtime, making static assignment of kernels to either PIM units or GPU-like compute accelerators suboptimal. Furthermore, existing PIM units are designed with a one-size-fits-all approach that fails to exploit the heterogeneity within memory-bound LLM kernels.
method: PAPI introduces a heterogeneous computing system combining PIM units embedded in DRAM with compute-centric accelerators (GPU-like), and a runtime that dynamically profiles kernel characteristics and remaps each kernel to the most suitable processing element at runtime. The PIM units are co-designed with awareness of intra-PIM heterogeneity to efficiently handle diverse memory-bound kernel patterns (e.g., matrix-vector products, attention, gating). A dynamic parallelism scheduler dispatches work to PIM or compute units based on real-time parameter changes driven by user or system demands.

title: Zettafly: A Network Topology with Flexible Non-blocking Regions for Large-scale AI and HPC Systems
problem: Post-exascale and zettascale AI/HPC systems require interconnection networks that support both scalability and non-blocking communication for concurrent jobs, but existing topologies (e.g., fat-tree, dragonfly) lack mechanisms to flexibly partition non-blocking sub-networks to match the small-to-medium job sizes that dominate compute-core-hour consumption in production systems.
method: Zettafly is a two-layer topology family: non-blocking groups (NB groups) at the bottom layer connected by global routers at the top, structured so that any minimally-routed packet between groups traverses at most one global router (low-diameter property). NB groups are sized and configured to match common job sizes, providing non-blocking communication within each group. The paper introduces simple adaptive routing algorithms tailored to Zettafly's structure and evaluates performance, cost, and scalability via extensive simulation against state-of-the-art topologies (fat-tree, dragonfly variants) under HPC workload traffic patterns including multi-task mixed traffic.

title: RAGO: Systematic Performance Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Serving
problem: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) serving is emerging as a critical LLM deployment pattern, but diverse RAG algorithm variants exhibit wildly different workload characteristics (retrieval latency, reranking compute, generation length), making a single optimization strategy inadequate. There is no systematic framework for characterizing and optimizing across the space of RAG pipelines.
method: RAGO introduces RAGSchema, a structured abstraction encoding the components and dataflow of any RAG algorithm, used to characterize and compare workload behaviors. The paper analyzes representative RAG variants with distinct schemas, exposing performance bottlenecks. RAGO then applies algorithm-specific system optimizations—scheduling policies, resource partitioning, and batching strategies—tuned to each RAGSchema's profile, rather than treating all RAG variants uniformly as extended LLM inference workloads.

title: FLAG: An FPGA-Based System for Low-Latency GNN Inference Service Using Vector Quantization
problem: Real-time GNN inference serving faces two bottlenecks: intensive preparation (neighbor aggregation, feature computation) and the neighborhood explosion problem (exponential neighbor set growth across layers), making it difficult to meet low end-to-end latency service level agreements.
method: FLAG offloads preparation to offline preprocessing, precomputing and compressing hidden embeddings via vector quantization. A dedicated FPGA accelerator ingests the precomputed data and performs lightweight online aggregation using the compressed embeddings, eliminating repeated computation.

title: Quartz: A Reconfigurable, Distributed-Memory Accelerator for Sparse Applications
problem: Sparse tensor and graph workloads exhibit irregular memory access patterns and variable computation densities that defeat fixed-dataflow ASIC accelerators designed for dense workloads. No single dataflow or memory organization handles the full diversity of sparse application kernels efficiently.
method: Quartz is a reconfigurable ASIC accelerator with distributed on-chip SRAM banks. The architecture exposes a programmable dataflow substrate that can be configured at runtime to match the access pattern of a given sparse kernel. Distributed memory banks reduce the bandwidth bottleneck by providing high aggregate internal bandwidth close to the compute units. A reconfigurable interconnect routes data between memory banks and processing elements according to the configured dataflow.

title: Revisiting Reliability in Large-Scale Machine Learning Research Clusters
problem: Large-scale ML training clusters suffer from frequent job failures whose impact on training efficiency is not well characterized across different job sizes and cluster configurations. Existing failure models do not adequately capture workload diversity or provide actionable metrics like Effective Training Time Ratio (ETTR).
method: The authors conducted an 11-month observational study across two large multi-tenant A100 GPU clusters totaling 4 million jobs and over 150 million GPU-hours. They developed a failure taxonomy, computed Mean Time to Failure (MTTF) as a function of GPU count by fitting a failure model to operational data, and derived an analytical estimator for Effective Training Time Ratio (ETTR) as a function of job parameters (checkpoint interval, restart overhead, failure rate). The ETTR model is used to project the efficacy of software mitigations such as more frequent checkpointing.

title: LegoZK: A Dynamically Reconfigurable Accelerator for Zero-Knowledge Proof
problem: Existing ZKP accelerators are designed at the granularity of core operators and exhibit low hardware resource utilization and limited adaptability across the different computation stages of proof generation (e.g., NTT, MSM, polynomial operations).
method: LegoZK uses finite field arithmetic units (FAUs) as fundamental building blocks integrated via a hierarchical on-chip NoC. By dynamically configuring the FAUs and the NoC interconnect at runtime, LegoZK can target each computation stage of proof generation without hardware specialization per stage. For the most time-consuming stage (Multi-Scalar Multiplication, MSM), LegoZK proposes a fast, fully pipelined bucket reduction algorithm based on lookup tables, significantly reducing MSM latency. The NoC topology and FAU configuration are switched between proof stages.

title: NetCrafter: Tailoring Network Traffic for Non-Uniform Bandwidth Multi-GPU Systems
problem: Hierarchical multi-GPU systems connect GPU groups with high-bandwidth intra-group links but lower-bandwidth inter-group links, creating severe performance bottlenecks on the inter-group network when traffic is not carefully managed. Conventional GPU communication treats all network flits uniformly, leaving bandwidth partially unutilized while also generating unnecessary traffic.
method: NetCrafter applies three complementary techniques to the inter-group network: (1) flit stitching, which coalesces partially-filled flits traveling to the same destination to maximize bandwidth utilization; (2) flit trimming, which drops speculative prefetch flits that are not yet needed, eliminating unnecessary traffic; and (3) flit sequencing, which reorders flits in the network so latency-sensitive critical flits reach their destinations ahead of bulk traffic, reducing effective latency for the most time-critical requests. The techniques are applied at the network boundary without modifying GPU compute pipelines.

title: vAttention: Dynamic Memory Management for Serving LLMs without PagedAttention
problem: PagedAttention enables dynamic KV cache allocation during LLM inference by breaking virtual memory contiguity, but this non-contiguous virtual memory layout for KV caches introduces non-trivial programming complexity and performance overheads in attention kernels and memory management logic. The changes to virtual memory layout require rewriting attention kernels and force suboptimal memory access patterns.
method: vAttention leverages OS virtual memory primitives (specifically, demand paging and virtual address space reservation) to provide contiguous virtual address spaces for KV caches while still allowing on-demand physical memory allocation. Instead of managing non-contiguous page tables in user space as PagedAttention does, vAttention reserves large contiguous virtual address ranges for KV caches upfront and relies on the OS to back them with physical pages on demand. This preserves contiguous virtual memory semantics seen by attention kernels, enabling use of standard (unmodified) CUDA attention kernels while still preventing physical memory fragmentation.

title: Hermes: Algorithm-System Co-design for Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation At-Scale
problem: As RAG datastores expand into the trillions of tokens, the retrieval phase dominates end-to-end latency and energy, undermining the benefits of using RAG to augment LLM outputs. Existing RAG systems lack mechanisms for efficiently routing queries to relevant subsets of a distributed datastore at scale.
method: Hermes partitions the RAG datastore across multiple nodes and uses a hierarchical search strategy that dynamically routes queries to relevant datastore subsets. A coarse-grained index tier rapidly identifies high-relevance partitions, and only those partitions are subjected to full dense retrieval (exact k-NN or approximate ANN). This co-design eliminates unnecessary retrieval computation on irrelevant partitions while maintaining retrieval quality.

title: Cassandra: Efficient Enforcement of Sequential Execution for Cryptographic Programs
problem: Modern out-of-order processors violate constant-time programming assumptions by transiently executing unintended control-flow paths, enabling Spectre-class transient execution attacks against cryptographic code. Existing mitigations that address control-flow misspeculations impose high performance overhead by broadly restricting speculative execution.
method: Cassandra disables branch prediction for constant-time cryptographic code regions and instead records and replays the deterministic sequential control flow using a Branch Trace Unit (BTU) added to the processor. Exploiting the observation that constant-time programs have mostly static control flow across runs and that cryptographic programs are loop-intensive with highly compressible control-flow patterns, Cassandra performs upfront branch analysis to compress control-flow traces stored in the BTU. The BTU then supplies fetch redirections from compressed trace storage, bypassing speculative branch prediction entirely for protected code regions.

title: SmoothE: Differentiable E-Graph Extraction
problem: E-graph extraction—selecting the optimal expression from a compact equality-saturation graph—suffers from an unfavorable scalability-quality trade-off: exact methods are slow, and fast heuristics produce suboptimal results. Current methods also only support simple linear cost functions, limiting applicability to realistic optimization objectives (e.g., non-linear, learned cost models).
method: SmoothE formulates e-graph extraction as a continuous, differentiable optimization problem by relaxing the discrete, combinatorial node-selection problem to a smooth objective over real-valued weights. Gradient-based optimization (e.g., gradient descent) is then applied to find the optimal extraction, enabling the use of arbitrary differentiable cost functions including learned neural cost models. The relaxation is designed so that the continuous optimum closely corresponds to a valid discrete extraction.

title: SEAL: A Single-Event Architecture for In-Sensor Visual Localization
problem: Traditional binary-encoded image sensors generate large data volumes that create energy and latency bottlenecks during transfer, storage, and processing for visual localization tasks such as keypoint detection and tracking. Moving these operations off-sensor to a host processor adds significant latency and energy cost.
method: SEAL introduces delay-based (temporal) codes at the pixel array level, replacing binary encoding with analog-to-time converters (ATCs) that represent pixel values as pulse delays (race logic). A temporal processor co-designed with the ATCs implements keypoint detection and tracking using race logic's single-wire-per-variable, single-event-per-wire policy, maximizing energy and area efficiency. A heavily quantized frontend processor then processes temporal outputs before the sensor-processor interface, enabling in-sensor VIO pipeline stages.
